## Background

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
The New Hospitals Programme (NHP) team are considering the impacts of single-bedded inpatient accommodation in it's planning assumptions. A notional figure of 12% reduction in length of stay was being assumed. The Strategy Unit was engaged to review the appropriateness of this figure.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
A rapid analysis of length of stay trends at Royal Liverpool Hospital (switched to single-bed accommodation in October 2022) was undertaken to assess the potential direction and scale of effect. The result of that initial crude analysis suggested some reduction was likely however there is significant potential that factors outside of the data may be influencing the effects, for example case-mix, hospital processes and pathways or wider ecological changes to inpatient demand.
:::
:::

## Official bed numbers...

There are several different published data sets that account for bed numbers in NHS hospitals:

-   KH03 returns
-   Bed Occupancy SitRep reports
-   Estates returns (ERIC)

Only ERIC (annual data collection) returns the number of Single Bed Rooms at NHS hospital sites, having done so since 2010/11. Previously it had reported the % of SBR rather than counts. The absolute number of (all) beds per site was only reported to 2014/15 making reliable ongoing measurement of SBR levels across the NHS difficult (read as impossible!).

Combining the SBR data from ERIC and KH03 (staffed) bed numbers suggest that overall in England, for NHS trust sites, the numbers of SBR have changed from 46,335 (`r round(46335/137151*100,1)`%) in 2010/11 to 56,449 (`r round(56449/130863*100,1)`%) in 2022/23.

Given this is a retrospective study, the debate on exactly what defines an NHS bed and how it is measured will not be addressed within our work - NHS England have established a working group to explore the issue going forward, information to be published shortly.

## Natural experiments

There are thought to be 8 schemes of similar nature in England where single-bed inpatient accommodation replaced multi-bed accommodation fully or in part. We will explore the feasibility of treating these intervention sites collectively or analysing them separately before producing combined estimates of effect.

## Proposal

The previous SU analysis highlighted the need for further work to better understand and quantify both the direct and indirect impacts of such a change to service model. This includes:

-   Targeted literature review of the nature and scale of impacts of changes like this
-   Impact analysis to quantify the (range of) effects on length of stay
-   Impact modelling of the indirect effects on non-length of stay metrics

Currently out of scope:

-   Patient sub-group impacts

## Literature Review

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
A previous systematic evidence review [@HEU2022] on the topic was commissioned by NHS England. The review aimed to identify significant clinical, humanistic and economic outcomes associated with admission to single-bed accommodation compared to shared rooms. The review grouped potential impacts into the following:

-   Clinical outcomes
-   Patient experience and satisfaction
-   Professional experience
-   Economic outcomes
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Conclusive findings were difficult to ascertain, though the review noted that patients generally preferred single rooms and length of stay savings may potentially offset increased costs of providing single-bed accommodation.
:::
:::

## Literature review update

The NHSE innovations team (\@ Joanne Wood) have created a 'living review' of evidence on this topic recently updated in January 2024 as well as specific reviews on e.g. Maternity admissions. No novel impacts have been identified although there may be important sub-groups to consider in the analysis including Neonate, Oncology, ICU and Frailty. As such, given the significant overlap, we feel there is no need for a comprehensive update to literature in support of this analysis.

However; there are still potentially a couple of gaps in respect of identifying other impacts for us to measure in our study or locating evaluative grey literature that may enhance validation of our findings. Identifying mitigating actions was discussed as another gap, however we believe is out of scope (or haven't resourced it within this plan) and should be considered as a follow-on exercise and/or separate commission.

Therefore we will execute a general internet search of literature related to impacts and use appropriate AI queries to exhaust the 'accepted wisdom' on impacts, their scale and to identify any appropriate case study candidates.

## Impact analysis

Questions of this type, where natural healthcare experiments are being assessed, are best addressed with some form of unit-level time-series analysis [@Clarke2019]. There are multiple options for this including:

-   Interrupted Time Series analysis (ITS)
-   Difference in Differences (DID)
-   Causal Impact Analysis (CIA)

## Method - Interrupted Time Series Analysis

Interrupted time series analysis (ITS), sometimes known as quasi-experimental time series analysis, is a method of statistical analysis involving tracking a long-term period before and after a point of intervention to assess the intervention's effects. Effects of the intervention are evaluated by changes in the level and slope of the time series and statistical significance of the intervention parameters. ITS analysis can be performed on data with or without control groups.

![](images/its_eg1.png){fig-align="center"}

## Method - Difference in Differences

Difference in differences is a statistical technique used to mimic an experimental research design using observational study data, by studying the differential effect of a treatment on a 'treatment group' versus a 'control group' in a natural experiment. It calculates the effect of a intervention on an outcome by comparing the average change over time in the outcome variable for the treatment group to the average change over time for the control group assuming on unobserved differences between groups.

![](images/did_eg1.png){fig-align="center"}

## Method - Causal Impact Analysis

CIA represents a relatively new technique [@broderson2015] with the specific aim of using control group(s) to estimate the post-intervention counterfactual against which to measure study group impacts. Selection of controls to account for similar hospital providers, similar catchment population, similar patient case-mix will be crucial.

CIA used in this way would also negate the need to collect significant amounts of explanatory variable data. More information on CIA can be found [here](https://research.google.com/pubs/archive/41854.pdf) and [here](http://google.github.io/CausalImpact/CausalImpact.html).

![](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5df3d68da6faaa72f61492dd/1581436264749-1XWAMQAAOTO7HGCT4NUB/Screen+Shot+2020-02-11+at+10.56.04+AM.png?format=2500w){fig-align="center"}

## Choice of method

Though all slightly different, each of the above methods would be appropriate for the requirements of this work.

On balance, we feel that CIA is the preferred method to deploy in this instance against a range of proxy outcome measures. This is principally due to the direct incorporation of control data into the counterfactual, it's inherent ability to infer significance as well as provide a range of effect sizes i.e. without the need to overlay bootstrapping or monte carlo simulation methods. The selection of control sites to calculate the counter-factual will be particularly crucial in this approach.

Should time/resource allow, and to compare & validate findings, we may apply all the above techniques to the same data.

## Choice of control sites

As mentioned above, the choice of control sites against which to compare changes in outcome variables post-switch to single-bed accommodation will be critical to the interpretation of the results. Each of the 7 sites in question changed accommodation type at different times and are likely to have a different set of controls.

We would aim to choose hospital sites that, for the period in question, match the study site in terms of:

-   size (levels of activity)
-   function [@eric]
-   demographic catchment (e.g. age and socio-economic profile)
-   patient case-mix (disease / morbidity / HRG profile)

If no clear and obvious control site/s emerge, we propose to use clustering or similarity analysis to find the n (3-5?) closest matching sites according to mixture of the above variables.

## Direct impacts

As identified in a previous review of literature on this topic [@HEU2022], the most commonly cited direct impacts of switching to single room accommodation are:

-   In or out of hospital mortality

-   In-hospital falls and fractures

-   Changes to length of stay (LoS)

-   Healthcare associated infection (HCAI)

-   Improved patient experience (sleep, privacy)

## Indirect impacts

Literature identified during our rapid analysis work suggests there are also likely to be unintended/indirect negative impacts of switching accommodation from multi to single beds that go beyond patient length of stays (ergo clinical improvement) and that should be part of a wider assessment of impacts. These may include, but are not restricted to:

-   Staff efficiency (moving between rooms and teamwork)

-   Overall productivity e.g. ability to manage waiting lists, recover occupancy from urgent care peaks

-   Patient loneliness

We will attempt to refine the recognition and definition of these factors or outcomes and aim to quantify them in the context of any given unit's size and activity and also, where possible, in respect of potential costs/savings.

```{r developing_proxy_measures, include = FALSE}

measures <- as_tibble(rbind(c("domain","id","desc","source","freq","time_period")
    , c("Health & Safety",1,"Summary Hospital-Level Mortality Indicator","https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/shmi","M","Dec18 to Aug23")
    , c("Productivity & Efficiency",2,"Length of Stay","SUS APCE, NCDR/UDAL","W/M/A","Apr08 to Nov23")
    , c("Health & Safety",3,"Healthcare Associated Infections","UKHSA (restricted)","-","-")
    , c("Patient or Staff Experience",4,"Patient experience","Friends and Family test, UKHF","M","Apr13 to Nov23")
    , c("Patient or Staff Experience",5,"Staff turnover","https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/nhs-workforce-statistics","M","Sept13 to Oct 2023")
    , c("Productivity & Efficiency",6,"Waiting Times","https://www.england.nhs.uk/statistics/statistical-work-areas/rtt-waiting-times/","M","Mar07 to Nov23")
    , c("Productivity & Efficiency",7,"Emergency readmissions","SUS APCE, NCDR/UDAL","W/M/A","Apr08 to Nov23")
    , c("Health & Safety",8,"In-hospital falls/fractures","SUS APCE, NCDR/UDAL","W/M/A","Apr08 to Nov23")
    , c("Productivity & Efficiency",9,"Occupancy levels","TBC, sitreps or KH03","M/Q","Mar20/Apr1998 to Dec23")
    , c("Patient or Staff Experience",10,"Sickness absence rates","https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/nhs-sickness-absence-rates/august-2023-provisional-statistics","M","Apr14 to Sept23"))
    , c("Productivity & Efficiency",11,"Cleaning staff WTE","https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/estates-returns-information-collection","A","2011-12 to 2022-23")) |> 
  row_to_names(row_number = 1)

```

## Proxy outcome measures

Given the collection of primary data is not in scope for this analysis, there is a requirement to identify existing routine and publicly accessible data that can act as relevant measures to assess changes over time before and after the move of any units to single-bed accommodation. The accuracy (specificity) of each proxy measure will be assessed and caveated during interpretation.

The following represent a summary of the metrics that we believe to me most relevant proxies for impacts identified by prior research or analysis and that are available from routine or publicly available data sources.

## Current proposed measures:

::: r-stack
**Health & Safety**
:::

```{r current_measures_HS}

measures |>
```

## Analytical plan

For each of the 7 hospital sites, undertake a controlled impact analysis against each of the 10? proxy outcome measures.

Where the 7 sites themselves are similar, it may be appropriate to pool the data to improve the power to detect changes over time. Either way, the output will be a ranged estimate of impacts for each measure and an indication of whether they might be increasing/sustainable/deteriorating effects.

Written report detailing data, methods and summary of key findings.

With agreement, code to be shared on github (either without data or with simulated data).
